extracted.intended_audience: teachers, teacher-trainers, and students of education (educational theorists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for educating and training the intellectual habit of reflective thinking in pupils — what thinking is, its constituent steps, and how teaching should cultivate disciplined, free, and experimental thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits of logical thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution, carefulness, thoroughness, definiteness, exactness, orderliness, methodic arrangement are the traits by which we mark off the logical from what is random and casual on one side, and from what is academic and formal on the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These traits distinguish the logical mind; cultivate habits that favor accuracy and definiteness rather than mere formality or casualness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual end of education
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole object of intellectual education is formation of logical disposition—namely, the formation of careful, alert, and thorough habits of thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the intellectual end (formation of thinking habits) as primary in intellectual education, distinct from moral ends; educational methods should aim to form these habits, not merely transmit facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false opposition of the psychological and the logical
rubrics_metrics.description: The psychological (natural) and the logical are not intrinsically independent or opposed; they are connected as earlier and later stages in one continuous process of normal growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat natural tendencies and logical training as mutually exclusive; the educator should transform natural powers (curiosity, inference, testing) into expert, tested powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between natural tendencies and subject-matter methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject both extremes: (a) methods that emphasize freedom, self-expression and ignore organized subject-matter; and (b) methods that rely wholly on subject-matter and external imposition (discipline as drill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid seeing method as merely devices to evoke native potentialities or as mere imposition of definitions and classifications; aim to coordinate natural activity with organized material so pupils develop internal logical habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter logic as goal, not starting point
rubrics_metrics.description: The logical from the standpoint of subject-matter represents the goal, the last term of training, not the point of departure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect immature minds to begin with adult-style divisions, definitions, and systems; gradually develop subject-matter logic from the child's existing modes of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the immature mind's own logic
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind at every stage of development has its own logic; natural activities already contain intellectual function and integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build on the child's existing curiosity, inference, experimenting, and testing rather than replacing them with ready-made logical schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline as result (trained independence), not coercive cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Discipline of mind is a result rather than a cause; it represents native endowment turned, through gradual exercise, into effective power—habitual power of effective mental attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for discipline that is positive and constructive (independent intellectual initiative and control), not mere externally imposed conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish genuine discipline from drill
rubrics_metrics.description: Discipline is frequently misregarded as drill—mechanical routine or forcible imposition leading to mental passivity and uniform external modes of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid methods that create mechanical routine, passivity, or servility; these do not develop habits of thinking even if they create outward conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine freedom is intellectual, not mere external spontaneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of mind means mental power capable of independent exercise, emancipated from the leading strings of others, not mere unhindered external operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate reflective control over impulses; do not equate freedom with uninterrupted spontaneous activity, which can foster unreflective behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstacles/perplexity are necessary for thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct immediate discharge of an impulse is fatal to thinking; only when an impulse is to some extent checked and thrown back upon itself does reflection ensue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cherish the natural difficulties that arise in activity as stimuli to reflective inquiry; there's no need to manufacture artificial problems when genuine obstacles exist in the material of experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form positive mental habits early
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive habits are being formed: either habits of careful looking, consecutive inquiry, and suspended judgment, or habits of hasty glancing, haphazard guessing, and credulity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise traits of carefulness, thoroughness, and continuity from the beginning; design conditions that call for and reinforce these habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five steps of reflective thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflection reveals five logically distinct steps: (i) a felt difficulty; (ii) its location and definition; (iii) suggestion of possible solution; (iv) development by reasoning of the bearings of the suggestion; (v) further observation and experiment leading to its acceptance or rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach pupils to progress through these steps; note that the first two may fuse and that the degree to which each step is pursued depends on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful definition/diagnosis before solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspended judgment and inquiry to determine the nature of the problem before attempting solution—definition of the difficulty is essential to critical thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage diagnosis (thorough inspection of the problem) to avoid premature fixation on the first suggestion; use examples (e.g., physician delaying acceptance of first hypothesis) to illustrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate multiple alternative suggestions (hypotheses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestion is the heart of inference and involves going from what is present to something absent; cultivation of a variety of alternative suggestions is an important factor in good thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote enterprising yet cautious habits of mind and the selection/arrangement of facts that give rise to richer, diverse hypotheses rather than a single premature conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoning to develop implications of an idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning develops the bearings or implications of any idea with respect to the problem; it sets out from an idea and traces what would follow from adopting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reasoning to test, refine, and transform tentative suggestions; rigorous tracing of consequences can reject unfit conjectures or make remote ideas apt and fruitful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental corroboration and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The concluding step is experimental corroboration: conditions are deliberately arranged according to an idea to see if the theoretically indicated results occur; observation at the end tests the hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that conjectures be checked by observation or experiment where possible; strong confirmation occurs when theoretical results are observed and no other conditions could produce them.

rubrics_metrics.name: The double movement of reflection: induction and deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflection involves a double movement: from partial, confused data to a suggested comprehensive whole (roughly inductive), and back from the suggested whole to the facts to connect and test them (deductive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach both movements—forming inclusive meanings from data and then deducing implications to seek confirmatory facts; both are essential parts of systematic inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trained judgment about the extent of steps
rubrics_metrics.description: The disciplined mind is the one that judges how far each step (observation, idea-formation, reasoning, testing) needs to be carried in any particular situation; no cast-iron rules can be laid down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop pupil ability to balance depth and expediency—know when prompt action is preferable and when prolonged inquiry is necessary, and learn from past mistakes to calibrate effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate thinking into everyday activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Thinking begins early and is present in everyday problem-solving (e.g., a child seeking a lost ball); the thought-factor already active in childhood must be made the most of for later reflective power to emerge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ordinary experiences as occasions for developing inference, testing, and reasoning rather than postponing intellectual training until adolescence.
